osi-model-deep-dive.core: The OSI model is a debugging map. Seven layers each have a job, an address type and a data unit; data is encapsulated layer by layer, and devices act on their own layer. Troubleshoot by isolating the failing layer, with the tool that tests that layer, from cables and frames up through routing, ports, TLS and application protocols.

first_principles.problem: Network problems get debugged by guessing instead of systematically.
truths: Each layer has its own failures.

analogy.title: A building inspection floor by floor
analogy.story: Start at the foundation and work up, testing each floor's systems.
analogy.breaks: Buildings are rigid; protocols blur layers.

check.q: What is the main practical use of the OSI model for engineers?
check.a: Systematically isolating which layer a network problem lives in and choosing the right tools to test it.

networking-protocols-tcp-udp-icmp-arp-dh.core: Five protocols underpin everyday networking: DHCP assigns identity, ARP maps IPs to MACs locally, ICMP reports errors and enables diagnostics and PMTUD, TCP provides reliable ordered streams governed by flow and congestion control, and UDP provides lightweight datagrams, now the base for QUIC and HTTP/3.

first_principles.problem: Without protocol knowledge, failures like no-lease, reset or slow transfers are mysteries.

analogy.title: Rules of the road
analogy.story: Registration, house numbers, road signs and delivery services together make the system work.
analogy.breaks: Roads are physical; protocols are negotiable software.

check.q: Which protocol failure causes large packets to vanish while small ones work?
check.a: Blocked ICMP 'fragmentation needed' messages breaking Path MTU Discovery.

dns-fundamentals.core: DNS is a hierarchical, delegated, cached database mapping names to records. Resolvers walk root → TLD → authoritative and cache by TTL. A, AAAA and CNAME map names, MX, TXT and SRV carry services and policy, and NS and SOA define delegation. Split-horizon tailors answers, anycast spreads servers globally, and DNSSEC plus DoH/DoT add integrity and privacy.

first_principles.problem: DNS is invisible until it breaks, and changes behave unexpectedly.

analogy.title: A global phone book with local copies
analogy.story: Copies speed lookups but take time to update.
analogy.breaks: Phone books are printed yearly; DNS caches expire in seconds to days.

example.title: Migration done right
flow: Lower TTL to 60 s a day early

check.q: Why do DNS changes not propagate instantly?
check.a: Resolvers cache records until their TTL expires, so old answers persist until then.

http-stack-fundamentals.core: HTTP is a stateless request/response protocol whose semantics (methods, status codes and headers) let browsers, proxies, caches and retries work correctly. Idempotency makes retries safe, TLS secures transport with key exchange and certificate identity, and browser security headers (CORS, CSP, HSTS) control what pages and scripts can do.

first_principles.problem: Misused HTTP semantics break caching, retries, security and monitoring.

analogy.title: A well-run postal system
analogy.story: Clear labels, honest receipts, signed deliveries and rules about who may open what.
analogy.breaks: Post is slow and physical; HTTP is fast and automated.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Safe retries, efficient caching, secure clients.

check.q: Why should APIs return accurate status codes instead of 200 with an error body?
check.a: Clients, proxies, retries and monitoring act on status codes, so wrong codes hide failures and break behaviour.

modern-web-protocols.core: HTTP/1.1's one-request-per-connection model caused head-of-line blocking and costly workarounds. HTTP/2 multiplexes binary streams over one TCP connection with HPACK header compression; HTTP/3 moves to QUIC to remove TCP head-of-line blocking and enable connection migration; and gRPC combines protobuf contracts with HTTP/2 for typed, streaming service-to-service calls.

first_principles.problem: Legacy protocols waste latency and make service contracts fragile.

analogy.title: From single-lane roads to smart highways
analogy.story: More traffic, fewer roads, independent lanes.
analogy.breaks: Highways have physical capacity; protocols also add CPU cost.

example.title: Upgrade path
flow: Internal services on gRPC via mesh

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Faster pages and typed internal APIs.

check.q: What does each HTTP version fix?
check.a: HTTP/2 fixes HTTP-level HOL with multiplexing; HTTP/3 fixes TCP-level HOL by using QUIC over UDP.

encrypted-dns-doh-dot.core: Plain DNS leaks and is easy to tamper with. DoT (TLS on 853) and DoH (HTTPS on 443) encrypt the client-to-resolver hop: DoT is simple and OS-wide but visible, DoH is camouflaged but can bypass enterprise controls. Encryption shifts trust to the resolver, so pick it carefully and use ODoH, canary domains and policies to balance privacy with control.

first_principles.problem: DNS reveals browsing and can be manipulated on-path.

analogy.title: Sealing your address-request postcards
analogy.story: Now only the recipient reads them, so choose that recipient wisely.
analogy.breaks: Postcards don't affect corporate mailrooms; DoH can.

check.q: Which encrypted DNS protocol is easier for networks to identify and block?
check.a: DoT, because it uses a dedicated port (853); DoH blends into HTTPS on 443.

vpc-architecture-fundamentals.core: A VPC is your isolated cloud network. Plan non-overlapping CIDRs and subnet them per AZ and tier; route tables make subnets public (IGW) or private (NAT or none); security groups (stateful) and NACLs (stateless) layer defences; admin access moves from bastions to SSM; and peering connects VPCs point-to-point, non-transitively, until Transit Gateway is needed.

first_principles.problem: Poorly designed VPCs block connectivity, waste money and expose systems.

analogy.title: Designing a gated estate
analogy.story: Lots, streets, gates, guards and bridges to neighbours.
analogy.breaks: Estates are permanent; VPCs are code.

check.q: What two things make a private subnet able to reach the internet outbound only?
check.a: A route for 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway (in a public subnet), and no public IPs on the instances.

global-routing-bgp-cdn.core: The internet is a network of autonomous systems that exchange reachability via BGP, a policy-driven path-vector protocol whose attributes (LOCAL_PREF, AS_PATH, MED, communities) let operators steer traffic, and whose trust model enables leaks and hijacks. On top, CDNs bring content close to users with PoPs, origin shields, careful invalidation and GeoDNS steering.

first_principles.problem: Global performance and reliability depend on routing and edge design most engineers never see.

analogy.title: Airline alliances and local warehouses
analogy.story: Routes depend on partnerships; goods are stocked near customers.
analogy.breaks: Airlines publish routes; BGP changes in seconds.

example.title: Global launch
flow: CDN with shield in front of origin

check.q: Which BGP attribute controls your outbound path, and which can hint inbound?
check.a: LOCAL_PREF controls outbound; MED, AS_PATH prepending and communities influence inbound.

advanced-bgp-security.core: BGP accepts claims on trust, which enables hijacks (false origins, more-specifics, forged paths) and leaks (routes escaping their scope). Defences layer RPKI (RIR-rooted certificates and ROAs with tight maxLength), route origin validation that drops Invalids, strict filters and roles against leaks, and Flowspec for surgical DDoS filtering.

first_principles.problem: A single bad announcement can disrupt or intercept traffic worldwide.

analogy.title: Adding passports and checkpoints to an honour system
analogy.story: Most travellers were honest, but now authority can be verified.
analogy.breaks: Passports are universal; RPKI coverage is still growing.

example.title: Secure network checklist
flow: ROAs for all prefixes, tight maxLength

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Hijacks of your space rejected widely.

check.q: What is the single most impactful step a network can take against hijacks?
check.a: Publish accurate ROAs for its prefixes and drop RPKI-invalid routes on import.

anycast-routing-fundamentals.core: Anycast announces one IP from many sites and lets BGP deliver each client to the nearest. That cuts latency by terminating connections close to users, splits DDoS traffic across global capacity, and fails over by withdrawing routes. Its catch is TCP state when routes shift, and GeoDNS is the finer-grained but cache-bound alternative.

first_principles.problem: Single-site services are slow far away and fragile under attack.

analogy.title: One phone number for a chain of branches
analogy.story: Callers reach the nearest open branch automatically.
analogy.breaks: Phones route by geography; BGP by topology.

check.q: How does an anycast site take itself out of service?
check.a: It withdraws its BGP announcement of the shared prefix, so traffic shifts to other sites.

internet-governance-iana-rirs-bgp.core: Internet governance coordinates unique identifiers without central ownership. IANA keeps global pools, the root zone and protocol registries; five RIRs allocate addresses and ASNs and run registry and RPKI services; BGP turns allocations into reachability; and peering and transit agreements determine paths, sometimes breaking through de-peering disputes.

first_principles.problem: Engineers rarely understand who controls addressing and reachability.

analogy.title: Postal coordination plus private couriers
analogy.story: A union assigns codes; private carriers decide routes by contract.
analogy.breaks: Couriers rarely refuse each other; networks sometimes do.

check.q: What are the three functions of IANA?
check.a: Managing number resources (IP/ASN pools), the DNS root zone, and protocol parameter registries.

ipv6-mastery.core: IPv6 replaces IPv4's exhausted 32-bit space with 128 bits, a /64 per LAN, and no broadcast. NDP over ICMPv6 handles discovery, SLAAC or DHCPv6 configure hosts, Happy Eyeballs makes dual-stack safe, NAT64/DNS64 let IPv6-only networks reach IPv4, and security needs equal policy on both stacks because global addresses are reachable without NAT.

first_principles.problem: IPv4 exhaustion forces NAT layers and blocks growth.

analogy.title: Upgrading to longer phone numbers
analogy.story: Everyone gets a direct line, with translators for old numbers.
analogy.breaks: Phones changed overnight; IPv6 coexists for decades.

check.q: What's the single biggest operational pitfall when enabling IPv6?
check.a: Forgetting to apply equivalent firewall/security policy to IPv6, leaving hosts exposed on their global addresses.

carrier-grade-nat-cgnat.core: CGNAT stretches scarce IPv4 by putting a second NAT inside the ISP, using 100.64.0.0/10 and sharing public IPs across many subscribers by port blocks. It breaks inbound port forwarding and P2P hole punching (strict NAT), and makes IP reputation shared. Escape routes are IPv6, outbound tunnels and overlays, VPS relays, or paying for a public IP.

first_principles.problem: IPv4 exhaustion pushes users behind shared addresses with broken connectivity.

analogy.title: A shared building address
analogy.story: Hundreds share one address; mail in is hard, mail out is fine.
analogy.breaks: Buildings have reception; CGNs drop unknown visitors.

check.q: What's the most sustainable long-term fix for CGNAT problems?
check.a: IPv6 deployment, which provides globally unique addresses without NAT.

load-balancing-physics.core: Load balancers spread work and hide failures. L4 balancers shovel packets per connection at high speed; L7 proxies parse requests to route and balance per request. Algorithms (round robin, least connections, P2C, consistent hashing) match workload shape; health checks with thresholds and outlier detection eject failures without cascading; and DSR lets egress-heavy services bypass the LB on return.

first_principles.problem: Single servers can't scale, and naive balancing causes hot spots and cascades.

analogy.title: Traffic officers and receptionists
analogy.story: Fast lane directors for volume, thoughtful receptionists for routing by purpose.
analogy.breaks: People adapt; LBs follow configured policy.

check.q: Why do large platforms often put L4 balancers in front of L7 proxies?
check.a: L4 handles massive packet volume cheaply and spreads load across the L7 fleet, which then does expensive per-request logic.

bare-metal-provisioning-pxe-ipmi-tinkerb.core: Bare-metal provisioning automates blank servers into working nodes. BMCs (IPMI, better Redfish) give out-of-band power and boot control, PXE uses DHCP and TFTP to load a small bootloader, iPXE switches to fast scripted HTTP boot, and engines like Tinkerbell model hardware and workflows declaratively so container-based actions install the OS.

first_principles.problem: Manual OS installs don't scale to fleets of physical servers.

analogy.title: A computer factory line
analogy.story: Machines roll in blank and roll out ready.
analogy.breaks: Factories see failures; firmware failures can be silent.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Rack provisioned in under an hour.

check.q: Why chain-load iPXE instead of using plain PXE/TFTP for everything?
check.a: TFTP is slow and static; iPXE fetches large images over HTTP and supports per-machine scripting.

cloud-connectivity-at-scale.core: Connecting many VPCs, regions and data centres needs a hub (Transit Gateway) with segmented route tables, encrypted VPNs (route-based, IPsec for gateways, WireGuard for hosts) for quick or backup links, and Direct Connect (dedicated or hosted) for predictable private bandwidth, with MACsec for line-rate link encryption.

first_principles.problem: Peering meshes and ad-hoc VPNs don't scale or segment.

analogy.title: Airport hubs with charters
analogy.story: Hubs for most routes, private charters for heavy ones.
analogy.breaks: Flights are scheduled; packets are routed instantly.

example.title: Enterprise network
example.outcome: connectivity that grows with the org.

check.q: What gives segmentation in a Transit Gateway design?
check.a: Separate TGW route tables with controlled associations and propagations per environment.

egress-cost-engineering.core: Egress is the hidden cloud tax. Costs climb from free (same-AZ, gateway endpoints) through cross-AZ and PrivateLink to NAT processing, cross-region and internet egress. NAT gateways silently tax AWS-bound traffic; gateway endpoints are free for S3 and DynamoDB, interface endpoints are cheaper than NAT at volume, and zone affinity keeps chatty services in-zone.

first_principles.problem: Data transfer bills rival compute because paths weren't designed for cost.

analogy.title: A car park with priced exits
analogy.story: Use free or cheap exits and avoid surcharged routes.
analogy.breaks: Car parks show prices; clouds bill later.

check.q: What's usually the fastest egress cost win in AWS?
check.a: Adding S3 (and DynamoDB) gateway endpoints so that traffic stops flowing through NAT gateways.

office-lan-networking.core: Office networks succeed on solid physical and L2 design. VLANs segment trust zones behind firewall policy, STP with BPDU Guard prevents loops, DHCP snooping and DAI stop rogue servers and spoofing, 802.1X authenticates devices with dynamic VLANs, Wi-Fi is designed for airtime capacity, and VPNs or ZTNA connect sites and remote users.

first_principles.problem: Flat, unprotected office networks are fragile and insecure.

analogy.title: A well-run office building
analogy.story: Separate rooms, badge doors, no tangled pipes, and secure links to other sites.
analogy.breaks: Buildings rarely change; networks change daily.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Stable and secure from day one.

check.q: Which two features stop a user's looped cable and a rogue DHCP router respectively?
check.a: BPDU Guard (with STP) and DHCP snooping.

high-performance-networking.core: At multi-gigabit rates, per-packet cost dominates. Interrupt coalescing and NAPI batch work, RSS spreads flows across cores, NIC offloads handle checksums and segmentation, jumbo frames shrink packet counts on internal networks, SR-IOV gives VMs direct NIC access, and DPDK bypasses the kernel entirely for the highest packet rates.

first_principles.problem: Default networking can't saturate fast NICs.

analogy.title: A Christmas post office
analogy.story: Machines, bundles, more counters and express lanes.
analogy.breaks: Post offices hire temps; servers don't.

check.q: Which technique distributes packet processing across CPU cores?
check.a: Receive Side Scaling (RSS), using multiple NIC queues bound to different cores.

high-speed-packet-processing-xdp-ebpf.core: The general-purpose kernel stack is too heavy for line-rate simple decisions. DPDK bypasses it at the cost of cores, tools and features, while XDP runs verifier-checked eBPF programs in the driver before sk_buff allocation, returning verdicts (drop, pass, tx, redirect) and sharing state via maps. It gets near-DPDK speed while keeping the kernel.

first_principles.problem: Simple per-packet decisions waste the full stack's cost.

analogy.title: A bouncer at the car park
analogy.story: Problems stopped before they enter; everyone else proceeds normally.
analogy.breaks: Bouncers judge; eBPF is verified code.

example.title: DDoS layer
flow: XDP program with LPM blocklist map
Control plane updates map from detections

check.q: Why can XDP be faster than iptables but safer than a kernel module?
check.a: It runs before sk_buff allocation, and the verifier proves the program can't crash the kernel.

tcp-ip-performance-tuning.core: TCP performance depends on matching the path. Size buffers to the bandwidth-delay product with window scaling, pick congestion control (BBR for long or lossy paths), fight bufferbloat with fq_codel or CAKE, save handshake RTTs with TFO or connection reuse, and tune methodically: measure, change one thing, re-measure.

first_principles.problem: Defaults leave long fat networks underused and queues bloated.

analogy.title: Filling a long pipeline without flooding the tap
analogy.story: Enough in flight to stay full, not so much it backs up.
analogy.breaks: Pipes don't ACK.

check.q: Which two settings most often limit single-stream throughput on long links?
check.a: Maximum socket buffer sizes (rmem/wmem) and the congestion control algorithm.

wireguard-internals.core: WireGuard is a minimal VPN: about 4,000 lines, fixed modern cryptography in a Noise_IK handshake, peers identified by public keys, and cryptokey routing that ties each key to allowed IP ranges for both routing and anti-spoofing. It's silent to scanners, handshakes on demand and roams seamlessly, and mesh control planes like Tailscale add key distribution, NAT traversal and ACLs.

first_principles.problem: Traditional VPNs are complex, slow and easy to misconfigure.
truths: Data plane needs a control plane at scale.

analogy.title: Simple locks with a smart key office
analogy.story: Locks are simple and strong; the office hands out keys and introductions.
analogy.breaks: Key offices are physical; control planes are online services.

check.q: What two jobs does AllowedIPs do in WireGuard?
check.a: Selects which peer to encrypt outbound packets to (routing) and validates inbound source addresses (access control).

network-verification-netdevops.core: NetDevOps replaces pray-and-deploy with software discipline: intent in a source of truth, generated configs in Git, Batfish-style models that simulate routing to prove reachability and isolation, differential analysis that shows the real impact of changes, and CI/CD pipelines with lab tests, staged deploys, rollback and drift detection.

first_principles.problem: Manual network changes cause most outages.

analogy.title: Flight simulators and assembly lines
analogy.story: Prove manoeuvres in the simulator, build with quality gates.
analogy.breaks: Simulators approximate; vendor bugs escape models.

check.q: What question can Batfish answer that a text diff cannot?
check.a: Whether the change alters which traffic is permitted or how it's routed, e.g. if any packet can now reach a protected subnet.

overlay-networking-vxlan-geneve.core: Overlays escape VLAN limits by encapsulating tenant traffic in UDP over a routed underlay. VXLAN (24-bit VNI, UDP 4789) is the standard; VTEPs with BGP EVPN learn locations without flooding; encapsulation adds about 50 bytes, so MTU must be managed by growing the underlay or shrinking the inner packets with MSS clamping; and Geneve adds extensible metadata options.

first_principles.problem: VLANs and stretched L2 don't scale to multi-tenant data centres.

analogy.title: Containers on rails
analogy.story: Standard containers carry any cargo over standard tracks.
analogy.breaks: Containers don't shrink cargo; MTU does.

check.q: What is the most common operational problem when introducing an overlay?
check.a: MTU mismatch from encapsulation overhead, causing large packets to be dropped.

sd-wan-sase-fundamentals.core: Costly, backhauled MPLS WANs gave way to SD-WAN: encrypted overlays on cheap diverse links, app-aware steering with path measurement, FEC and duplication, and local SaaS breakout. SASE then moves security (SWG, CASB, FWaaS, ZTNA) to global cloud PoPs with identity-based zero-trust policy, so protection follows users and sites anywhere.

first_principles.problem: Legacy WANs are expensive, slow for cloud apps, and tied to HQ security.

analogy.title: Smart satnav plus local airport security
analogy.story: Best route per vehicle and the same checks everywhere.
analogy.breaks: Airports are physical; PoPs are virtual.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Lower cost, faster SaaS, stronger security.

check.q: Why does SD-WAN local breakout create a need for SASE?
check.a: Traffic no longer passes HQ's security stack, so inspection and policy must move to cloud PoPs near users.

service-mesh-fundamentals.core: A service mesh moves cross-cutting network concerns out of application code. A data plane of proxies (sidecars, or eBPF and per-node proxies) applies mTLS, routing, retries and telemetry; a control plane computes and pushes xDS config and SPIFFE identities; and teams gain zero-trust service security, canary traffic shifting and uniform observability.

first_principles.problem: Microservices duplicate network logic inconsistently across languages.

analogy.title: Building utilities for services
analogy.story: Shared power, security and monitoring for every office.
analogy.breaks: Utilities are cheap; meshes cost resources.

check.q: What's the difference between the mesh data plane and control plane?
check.a: The data plane (proxies) handles every request; the control plane computes configuration and certificates and pushes them to proxies.
